I'll provide some general advice as I assume you don't want to show your channel for privacy sake. A view counts as someone watching beyond 30 seconds, so besides a good thumbnail and title, you might have a boring hook or an entirely boring idea. If your channel is mainly using videogames only as background footage, then add a variety of other b-roll content to start with. Faceless youtubers like Degenerocity and Dunkey are very good at utilizing b-roll to build interest.  Facecam is a good start but it's considered 'A-roll' which means it's meant to be used sparingly -- you can try acting out skits or doing something more with your camera. Consider your video's introduction -- most people want a quick summary or promise within the first 8 seconds and even the kindest of souls will click off very fast if the video feels boring (I blame our attention span for that). You do not need to stick to a niche so tightly until you have an audience demanding for it, so I highly recommend branching out and exploring what kind of ideas you want to make, balanced with what kind of content would catch people's interest. Ex: If you want to talk about how mental health education is important, you can discuss it in a video like "Gen Z is getting dumber", or "Ozempic Showed that Body Positivity Is a Lie"  to start with something interesting, but definitely look into the actual trends youtubers are discussing cuz I made up those topics in my head. In terms of personality, if you do have opinions about something controversial, you better make sure that they make sense because the last thing I want happening is an Andrew Tate clone to start yapping dogshit on youtube all because I gave advice on a subreddit. If you intend to be unbiased, keep in mind that while sensitive topics should be discussed, sometimes a topic is so controversial that you really cannot present both sides without sounding insane -- for example, please do not say slavery was a bad AND good thing. Also, while everyone is unique, only a small percent of youtubers have an actual great personality -- somebody like MoistCritikal or Dunkey who posts seemingly easy to make videos succeeds because they have an entertaining personality and character that makes up for it. The average youtuber like me has to cope with their average boring personality and build trust/loyalty with their audience overtime to reach that kind of success, so bear in mind it will probably take longer than expected to find a connection with your viewers. (I also want to point out that you do not need to change your personality just to please people, in fact the longer you make videos, the more comfortable you will likely feel in expressing yourself online) Lastly, you mention that you are already gaining subscribers and impressions, so I really think you must keep improving on making thumbnails and titles. It's normaI for this kind of slow growth to happen since I think my first 2 weeks of my videos had either 50 views or 0, and continued until I started looking for trends which boosted my videos to 100-200 views. Half a year later, I got monetized last month, so I will stress that being a youtuber continues to dig on your mental health no matter how successful you are,. That's why my last point is that you should take care of yourself vigilantly. You prolly already know but all that good shit like gratitude, self-management, taking breaks will benefit your channel  & more importantly your life solely because doing youtube subtracts from your health and time on this earth. Rember that an unsuccessful youtube channel does not mean that the public hates you or anything personal like that. You mentioned that you do not use AI, your subscribers are fairly loyal, and watch time is good -- any of those three aspects are enough to pat yourself on the back and keep improving.

A simple structure that usually holds attention:

• 0–1s: very specific promise (“3 signs your nervous system is overloaded after birth…”)

• 1–10s: deliver 1 concrete point fast (no long intro)

• 10–25s: 2nd point + example

• 25–35s: 3rd point + what to do next

• Last 2s: CTA to a series (“Part 2 tomorrow: what helped me most…”) to drive follows

I have a faceless channel with about 94k subs.  I've definitely felt the pressure to come up with a bunch of images/art/b-roll as a result - sometimes having over 100 assets in a 10-minute video.  What I've found with my content (and it could be different for everyone), is that viewers who are genuinely interested in the content don't seem to care if you have 100 art assets, or 10.  My experience is that *we* care about it way more than *they* do.

To fight the urge to do too much, I have a strict budget of 1 hour per 3 minutes of my final video.  That's everything, except for research.  It makes me go way more bare-bones on editing and art than would be my natural inclination.  

As for the time savings from showing your face, I'd actually say that it's probably less than you think.  It's way easier to edit your audio when you don't have the video component.  Once you're on camera, the additional consideration is that you need to get a clean, continuous take - at least for significant sections of dialog.  For people who don't do that, the editing looks very disjointed - and it's super obvious to the viewers.

If you're looking for additional ideas, your b-roll doesn't need to be directly relevant.  Stock images, stock video, and even things like FDM timelapse videos can fill in sections where you're talking.

for a military channel your best friend is public domain government footage. DVIDS (dvidshub.net) is the department of defense media hub and basically everything on it is public domain because it's federal work, same with the national archives and NASA. you can use that freely, no copyright strike, and a lot of faceless military channels are built on exactly that.

  
for generic b-roll, pexels, pixabay and mixkit are free and license-clear, just actually read the license on each clip because a few have restrictions.

  
two things that actually get people struck, since footage is rarely the real problem:

  
\- music. that's where most content ID claims come from, not video. use youtube's own audio library or something like uppbeat and you're fine.

the reason your own voice sounds awful is that youve heard it your whole life through your own skull, so theres a load of low end in it that literally nobody else hears. the recording is what you actually sound like to everyone else, your brain just hasnt caught up. thats why it feels like youre being mocked, its uncanny to you and only you. everyone else just hears a normal person talking.

and everyone hates theirs at first, properly everyone. it does get easier, but mostly just because you stop noticing it, not because you wake up loving the sound. first handful of voiceovers are rough then you stop hearing yourself.

two things that genuinely help. dont relisten to your own audio over and over while you edit, do one pass and move on, the obsessive replaying is what wrecks you. and record like youre explaining the footage to a mate sat next to you, not like youre "doing a voiceover". the put-on presenter voice is the bit that makes you cringe, your actual talking voice is fine.

text on screen and music is a real format, loads of faceless channels do alright on it, but ill be honest its harder to hold someone for ten minutes on footage and captions than with a voice carrying them. if youre serious about long form, pushing through the voice thing is the highest payoff move youve got, way more than any editing trick. its just uncomfortable for a few videos. for this one though, youve got 5 hours, you could cut it really tight and let the footage do the work with text only where something actually needs explaining. that gets a proper long video out the door while you get used to hearing yourself for the next.

voiceover with screen recordings and still shots honestly, that combo kills it for faceless channels. been running a tech channel without showing myself for like three years now and the trick is just accepting that youre gonna lean harder on motion graphics, text overlays, and like 30 second clips of the actual product or process rather than trying to film everything. people watch for the info and personality in your voice, not your mug, so spend less time chasing perfect broll and more time on what actually matters, the narration and pacing. instaboost helped stabilize my reach when algorithm changes hit, but the real growth came from just accepting the format constraints and working within them instead of fighting them.

aim for like 60% screen recordings or product footage, 30% graphics and text, 10% actual broll when you can get it. thats the ratio ive seen work best in educational spaces where youre not the main visual. sounds lazy but it actually frees you up to make more videos, and consistency beats perfection every time on youtube. your four videos in two months is honestly decent pacing if theyre solid, so dont burn yourself out trying to match creators who are showing their face and cruising on personality.
